newsitem.title: ITALY: Lira rate puts pressure on Italy in EMU process.
newsitem.headline: Lira rate puts pressure on Italy in EMU process.

text.p: The lira's new central parity of 990 per mark in the Europe Union's currency grid puts greater pressure on Italy to get its public finances into order and fight inflation, independent economists said.

In their first reaction after agreement by EU Finance Ministers on the lira's return to the exchange rate mechanism after four years, they said the currency was likely to trade towards the new rate but would not strengthen beyond it.

Lorenzo Codogno, chief economist at Bank of America in Milan, said the stronger lira was the price the Italian economy had to pay in order to gain more credibility in moving towards taking part in European economic and monetary union (EMU).
"It puts on even more pressure for fiscal discipline and for having inflation under control," Codogno said.

He expected the currency to trade up to 990 per mark initially with the market drawn to the new level, while Lorenzo Stanca at Credito Italiano saw 990 as the ceiling for the currency's strength at the start.
After that, they said the lira's path would depend on the dollar and the mark and the outlook for Italian interest rates.
Pio De Gregorio, economist at NatWest Markets in Milan, said he expected the lira to trade between 990 and 1,000 against the mark initially then at 1,000 in the near term.
"Further out it depends crucially on what the government will be able to deliver in terms of budget consolidation and inflation convergence," De Gregorio said.
He said the government would now have to move swiftly to reform pensions and welfare spending to make structural reforms to reduce its budget deficit.
Retaining credibility on the deficit and inflation was key to keeping the lira stable and close to its new parity as the option of raising interest rates was not on offer, he said.
The government wants to keep rates down not only to keep the economy ticking over but also to contain interest payments and therefore the budget deficit.
The outlook for interest rates, was mixed with Codogno saying the parity increased the chances that the Bank of Italy would make an expected cut in the key discount rate near term.

"If the lira stays close to this 990 level then it's more likely the Bank of Italy will cut. If we have a strong lira near term then it could cut in the next few days but the Bank of Italy will want to see the market reaction," Codogno said.
But Stanca at Credito said: "It is going to be kind of tough for the Bank of Italy to cut rates immediately in the next few weeks because of this parity."
He expected the central bank to wait to see how the currency fared and then to consider cutting in a month's time.

Both Stanca and De Gregorio said the chosen parity was stronger than their assessment of the lira's purchasing power parity, and De Gregorio expected Italian industry, which has openly said it wanted a central rate of 1,050, to protest.
He said the new parity was likely to influence government negotiations with metalworkers' unions on new contracts.

"Low wage growth becomes paramount to keep the government's economic policy standing. Industry will use this argument to convince the government the wage requests of the metalworkers are not consistent with the fixed parity," De Gregorio said.
Profit margins would also be pressured. "For manufacturers it will be more important in the future to control costs - and labour costs are among the most important," he said.
